parsed_response.reasoning: Verified: in parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts the schema uses `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` as computed keys. Zod schema objects have no toString override, so both keys become the literal '[object Object]', colliding into one property; the effective schema only requires access_token (plus a bogus '[object Object]' field, likely also failing parse when absent — either way, other fields like refresh_token/instance_url/expiry are not captured or are stripped by zod's default strip mode). Line 26 then writes `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = 'refresh_token'` on success. The diff also shows callers (Zoom `parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, zoomRefreshedTokenSchema)`, Office365, Google, Salesforce) persisting this parsed result to prisma.credential, so in credential-sharing mode stored credentials lose fields (e.g. Salesforce drops instance_url), corrupting subsequent refreshes. The described mechanism matches the diff exactly.

judged_text: The computed schema keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] both evaluate to the single literal property name "[object Object]" (ZodString defines no toString override), so minimumTokenResponseSchema validates only access_token while Zod's default strip mode discards every other response field, after which line 26 writes the literal string "refresh_token" into the parsed data. In credential-sharing mode every caller persists credentials reduced to {access_token, refresh_token:"refresh_token"} — Zoom and Office365 spread that literal over their stored key, and Salesforce stores a two-field key that drops instance_url, so the next service construction reads undefined instance_url/refresh_token; if the operator later disables sharing, refresh requests send the literal "refresh_token" and those integrations are permanently bricked.
